wolffish.title: Wolffish
wolffish.subtitle: Runtime behavior. Off by default — turn things on as you trust them.

launchAtStartup.label: Launch at startup
launchAtStartup.description: Automatically start Wolffish when you log into your computer. When enabled, Wolffish registers itself as a login item with your operating system — macOS, Windows, and Linux are all supported. This lets Wolffish be ready the moment your session begins, so you can jump straight into a conversation without opening it manually. Disable this if you prefer to launch Wolffish only when you need it.

blockCredentials.label: Block sensitive data in messages
blockCredentials.description: When enabled, messages that appear to contain passwords, API keys, tokens, or private keys are immediately discarded — they never reach the agent, are never stored, and you get a short notification instead. Off by default so the agent can freely discuss credentials when needed. Turn it on if you want a hard guard against accidentally pasting secrets into chat.

bypassPermissions.label: Bypass permissions mode
bypassPermissions.description: When enabled, all tool actions auto-approve without showing the approval dialog. The amygdala still classifies every action and logs everything to the corpus event bus and feedback files exactly as before — only the human approval step is skipped. Use this for trusted environments where you want full agent autonomy. Disable it any time to restore manual approval.

restrictPowerfulModels.label: Restrict powerful local models
restrictPowerfulModels.description: When enabled, the model picker blocks local models whose memory footprint exceeds what your system can handle comfortably (~55% of total RAM). This prevents severe slowdowns, swap thrashing, and system instability caused by loading oversized models. Turning this off lets you install and run any model regardless of hardware limits — not recommended. Oversized models force your system into heavy disk swapping, making both Wolffish and your entire machine unresponsive.

voiceReplies.label: Voice replies
voiceReplies.description: When you send a voice prompt, Wolffish replies with a spoken voice memo. Files and text still arrive when the work needs them — the reply just ends spoken aloud. This switch alone controls whether the model is instructed to do this. Turn it off to get text replies to voice prompts.

weekStartsOn.label: Start of week
weekStartsOn.description: Sets the day Wolffish treats as the first day of the week. Drives how the activity heatmap is laid out and how date ranges like "this week" line up in your head. Default is Monday (the ISO 8601 standard most of the world uses); pick Sunday if your calendar app and routines start there. Internal weekly memory files keep their existing ISO-week names so older summaries don't shift.

reflection.title: Reflection
reflection.subtitle: Every night, Wolffish reviews its finished conversations — what worked, what failed — and distills the lessons into a playbook it carries into every future turn.

nightly.label: Nightly reflection
nightly.description: Reviews every conversation that has settled since the last pass — automations included — scoring each one and extracting what worked, what failed, and what you liked. The lessons fold into the playbook carried into every turn. Missed fires (asleep, app closed) run on the next launch.

quiet.label: Review after quiet for
quiet.description: A conversation is only reviewed once it has been idle this long, so unfinished work isn't judged early. Anything still warm simply waits for a later night — nothing is ever skipped — and a conversation you continue after its review gets reviewed again with the new turns included.

deepClean.label: Monthly deep reflection
deepClean.description: Once a month, a deep reflection takes the opposite stance of the nightly pass: it challenges the playbook and knowledge files against recent evidence, merging duplicates and pruning stale, over-general, or contradicted entries — the structural guard against learned bad habits.

reflection.runStarted: Started — the result card updates when it finishes.

daily.description: Extracts key facts from today's conversations and saves them to knowledge files.

weekly.description: Merges the week's episode logs into a single digest for archival.

guide.title: What you can drop
guide.skillDesc: A markdown procedure with a YAML frontmatter block (name, description, and optional triggers). Imported as a pure skill — guidance the agent follows when a trigger matches, with no tools or dependencies to install.
guide.folderDesc: A folder containing a SKILL.md alongside an optional plugin/ (index.mjs) and package.json. This is the full capability — the skill, its executable tools, and any declared dependencies, all in a single drop.
guide.zipDesc: The same capability folder, compressed into one file. It's safely unpacked to a temporary location, validated exactly like a folder, then added only once every check passes.
guide.tip: Every drop is fully validated before anything is written to disk, so a failed import can't corrupt or half-install your existing capabilities. The name must be unique across all capabilities, and any system or npm dependencies are installed automatically the first time the capability runs.

cli.title: CLI
cli.subtitle: Wolffish in a terminal. The same agent, the same settings, the same conversations — no window needed, which is what lets it run on a server you reach over SSH.

verbose.label: Show all tool activity
verbose.description: On prints every tool call and its result in the terminal, plus the model chip. Off prints only the agent's replies, the files it delivers, and anything that failed.

path.title: The wolffish command
path.shadowed: Another program named "wolffish" comes first on your PATH — this is usually the desktop app itself, linked by the package manager. Running the command will open the app instead of the terminal session. Move {{dir}} ahead of it, or remove the other link.
path.needsEntry: Its folder is not on your PATH yet. Add this line, then open a new terminal:
path.needsEntryDone: Its folder was added to your shell profile. Open a new terminal window and the command is there.
path.hint: Wolffish writes this automatically on every launch, so it stays pointed at the current version after an update.

toast.needsPath: Installed — add its folder to your PATH
toast.openTerminal: Command installed — open a new terminal to use it

service.title: Start on its own
service.description: Wolffish registers itself with the operating system so it comes back after a restart — automations fire, channels answer, and the terminal attaches whenever you want one. This is the same setting as Launch at startup; changing it here changes it there.

gui.label: Login item
gui.description: Starts when you log in, and opens the window. Needs a desktop session, so it never fires on a server.

headless.label: Background service
headless.description: Starts with the machine, with no session and no window. This is what a server wants, and what the terminal attaches to.

service.headlessHostHint: This machine has no desktop session, so a login item will never fire here. Choose the background service.
service.sameAsPreferences: This is the same switch, so changing it here changes it there. What this card adds is the choice of mechanism, which only matters when you run without a window.

confirm.title: Run as a background service?
confirm.body: A background service is registered to stay running: if you quit Wolffish, the system starts it again within a few seconds. That is what a server wants — automations keep firing and channels keep answering with nobody logged in — but on a machine you use directly it means the app will not stay closed.
confirm.reversible: You can switch back to a login item, or turn autostart off entirely, from this same card at any time.

daemon.title: The terminal is a view, not the app
daemon.body: Wolffish runs as a background process. The command attaches to it and detaches when you leave — close the terminal, or lose the SSH connection, and the agent keeps working. Come back and it reattaches to whatever is still running.

files.title: Files are paths, both ways
files.body: Attach with a path; a delivered file prints its own path, ready to open or copy. Nothing is uploaded or encoded, because the terminal and the agent share one filesystem.

settings.title: Every setting on this screen
settings.body: The command reads and writes the same settings these panels do, through the same code. Anything you can change here you can change there, with the same label and description.

approvals.title: Approvals wait for you
approvals.body: A tool call that needs approval pauses and asks in the terminal. If you disconnect first, it waits — you can answer when you come back, or from your phone.

services.subtitle: Tools and integrations that extend what Wolffish can do.

gate.errorBody: The {{name}} capability hit a problem while loading, so these settings are disabled for now. The error is shown below, and the Capabilities page has the full picture.

howItWorks.step1: A blue glow, a notice and a shadow cursor appear on the display while the agent works — the shadow cursor glides to every target before the action, and your own pointer stays yours.
howItWorks.step2: Clicks, typing and shortcuts are posted straight to the target window in the background; when an app refuses, the agent switches to a brief foreground delivery and says so.
howItWorks.step3: It finds controls by name through the app's accessibility tree and clicks them by reference, or zooms into small targets at native resolution — never guessing.
howItWorks.step4: Every action returns evidence: how it was delivered, the control found under the point, an objective before-and-after screen comparison, and whether your mouse moved during it.
howItWorks.step5: It checks the permissions this machine grants before starting and tells you the exact setting to enable when one is missing.
howItWorks.step6: It chooses each capture's resolution and format itself — sharper when it must read detail, lighter when it only navigates. Ask for a higher-resolution screenshot any time.

debuggerMode.title: Debugger Mode
debuggerMode.body: Wolffish uses Chrome's debugger API to simulate human-like browser interactions (clicks, typing, scrolling) that are indistinguishable from real user input. This works automatically on all Chromium-based browsers — Chrome, Brave, Edge, Arc, Opera, and Vivaldi. No setup is required.
debuggerMode.infobarNote: When debugger mode is active, a yellow infobar saying "Extension is debugging this page" may appear at the top of the tab. This is a standard Chrome notification and is purely cosmetic — it does not affect functionality. To hide it, launch your browser with the following flag:
debuggerMode.tipText: Create a separate browser shortcut with this flag for Wolffish automation sessions.
debuggerMode.notSupportedText: Firefox and Safari do not support the debugger extension API. Debugger mode is Chromium-only.

browserExtension.readinessSubtitle: What Wolffish needs to drive your browser, and what to do about anything missing.
browserExtension.readinessReady: Everything Wolffish needs is in place.

video.title: Video generation
video.subtitle: Generate video with MiniMax H3 from text, images, frames, or reference media.
video.apiKeyHint: The same MiniMax key you use elsewhere works here; it is stored separately on purpose — see below.
video.testSuccess: Key accepted — video generation is ready

separateKey.title: Why this key is separate from the MiniMax chat provider
separateKey.p1: MiniMax issues one credential that unlocks both its chat models and its video API, so the value you paste here is the same string you may already have under Settings → Providers → MiniMax. The app deliberately does not copy one into the other, and you need to fill in both.
separateKey.p2: They are independent decisions. Video generation is a service — like Brave search or Giphy — not a property of whichever brain you are chatting with. If the keys were shared, switching your chat brain to another provider and clearing the MiniMax entry would silently break video generation, and rotating a key for one use would drag the other along with it.

howItWorks.title: How it works
howItWorks.p1: MiniMax H3 never appears in the model picker, because you never chat with it. It is a tool your current model calls. Generation is asynchronous — the API hands back a task id and renders for a few minutes — so the app manages that lifetime for you.
howItWorks.s1: Ask for a video in any conversation. Your current model calls the video tool with a prompt it writes itself.
howItWorks.s2: A task card appears in the chat with the task id, live status and a progress estimate. It updates itself; you can cancel from the card.
howItWorks.s3: The finished mp4 is downloaded automatically and plays inline in the card.
howItWorks.s4: Your model then delivers the file — in the app, or to Telegram / WhatsApp when the conversation came from there (oversized videos are compressed to fit, with the original kept here at full quality).
howItWorks.footer: If a generation outlives its turn — the app restarts, or the model moved on — the app finishes the job on its own: it keeps polling, saves the video, updates the card, and sends it to the channel it came from.

director.title: Your chat model is the director
director.p1: The video model does not read your request. Your selected chat model does, and rewrites it into a full cinematic prompt — subject, camera movement, lighting, mood — then chooses duration, resolution, aspect ratio, and which images act as first frame, last frame or style reference. That rewriting is where most of the quality comes from.
director.askExample: a 4 second video of gentle ocean waves rolling onto a beach at sunset
director.promptExample: Gentle ocean waves rolling onto a sandy beach at sunset. Soft golden-orange light reflecting off the water, calm ripples of foam washing up the shore and receding. Slow, soothing motion, warm pastel sky with hints of pink and amber near the horizon, a few scattered clouds catching the last light. Cinematic, serene, photorealistic, gentle push-in camera barely moving.
director.b1: It adds the creative detail you left out — light, texture, atmosphere, camera language — because sparse prompts produce flat, generic footage.
director.b2: It picks the technical settings from context, and omits the aspect ratio when you supply an image so the video adopts the picture's own shape.
director.b3: It names the task, waits for the render, and decides how to present the result to you.
director.footer: A stronger chat model writes a better prompt and gets a better video from the identical request. If a clip misses what you pictured, telling your model what to change is usually more effective than rewording your original ask.
director.currentHint: This is whichever model you chat with — switch it from the composer and the next video is directed by the new one.
director.offHint: Director mode is off — your request is sent to the video model exactly as you wrote it. The model still picks duration and resolution unless you specify them.

capabilities.title: What H3 can do
capabilities.p1: One model, four input modes — combine them freely, up to twelve media items in a single request.
capabilities.modes: Text to video · image to video (first frame) · first-and-last frame transition · reference images, clips and audio for consistent subjects, motion and voice.
capabilities.output: H.264 mp4 with a generated soundtrack, 24 fps, 768P or 2K, 4 to 15 seconds. Rendering typically takes one to five minutes.
capabilities.limits: Media you attach is checked and optimized automatically — oversized images are downscaled, unusual video and audio formats are converted — so requests fit the API's limits without you resizing anything.
capabilities.storage: Videos are saved per conversation under generations/video in the workspace, and deleted with the conversation.
capabilities.footer: You can also attach a media URL from the composer's paperclip menu instead of a file; MiniMax fetches it directly, which sidesteps the request size limit for large references.

mcp.title: MCP
mcp.subtitle: Connect Model Context Protocol servers to give Wolffish new tools.

how.title: How this works
how.add: Add a connection with a command (for servers that run on this machine) or a URL (for remote servers). Wolffish connects right away — no restart, no setup steps. If a server requires sign-in, you'll see one button for it here.
how.tools: Everything a connected server offers becomes available to Wolffish on your very next message, in normal chat and to workflow agents alike.
how.background: Wolffish keeps each connection healthy on its own: it checks in periodically, reconnects with steadily-spaced retries if one drops, refreshes a server's tools whenever it reconnects, and keeps every connection isolated so one failing never touches another.
how.offline: If a server crashes or drops offline, its tools quietly step aside while Wolffish reconnects in the background. Nothing breaks, and there's nothing you need to do.

mobile.title: Mobile
mobile.description: Run Wolffish on your phone as a companion to this desktop — the same conversations, settings and usage, over an end-to-end encrypted tunnel. The app is built from source and the relay is yours to run; the steps are below.

setup.title: Set it up yourself
setup.intro: The phone app is no longer in the App Store or Google Play, and the relay it used to connect through is gone. Everything you need is in the Wolffish repository: a relay you deploy, an app you build and install, and one pairing.

relay.title: Deploy the relay
relay.body: Open packages/relay in the repository and follow its README. A free Cloudflare account and about ten minutes give you a wss:// address of your own; any machine that runs Node works too.

address.title: Enter the relay address here
address.body: Paste the wss:// address into the Relay card below and click Use this relay. The next pairing carries it to your phone, so nothing is typed there.

build.title: Build the app from source
build.body: Open apps/mobile in the repository, run npm install, and put your own app identifier into app.config.ts (plus your Expo account if you build on EAS). The README names the exact lines.

install.title: Install it on your phone
install.body: iPhone: plug it in and run npm run ios:device from a Mac with Xcode. Android: npm run android with USB debugging on, or npm run android:apk on EAS for an APK you sideload.

pair.title: Pair
pair.body: Generate a QR below, open the app, tap Connect to Desktop and scan it. From then on the phone reconnects by itself.

setup.footer: Push notifications while the app is closed need one more thing: an access token from your Expo account, stored on your relay. The relay README covers it. Without it, notifications still arrive whenever the app is open.

mobile.notPaired: No phone is paired yet. Once the app is on your phone and your relay address is set, start a pairing here, then open Wolffish on the phone and connect.
mobile.qrDesc: Generate a QR and scan it with your phone's camera. The secret travels screen to camera — it never crosses the network.
mobile.codeDesc: Generate a short code and type it on your phone — for when the camera can't see this screen.
mobile.codeDescCustomRelay: Generate a short code and type it on your phone along with your relay's address — the code alone can't carry it. The QR does this for you.
mobile.scanHint: Open Wolffish on your phone, tap Connect to Desktop, and scan this code.
mobile.codeHint: Type this code on your phone — case and dashes don't matter.
mobile.codeRelayHint: Your phone must use the same relay — enter this address in the Relay card on its pairing screen:
mobile.fingerprintHint: Matching values on both devices mean nothing sits in between.

how.title: How it works
how.pairBody: The QR or code carries a one-time secret. Each device keeps its own key and pins the other's — no account, no password.
how.e2eBody: Everything is sealed on your devices before it is sent (X25519 · ChaCha20-Poly1305). Only this desktop and your phone hold the keys.
how.relayBody: The relay only helps the two devices find each other and passes sealed bytes along. It cannot read, alter or replay them, and it stores nothing — no database, no logs, no accounts, no message history.

relayConfig.body: Where the two devices meet to exchange sealed frames. There is no hosted relay: deploy the one in packages/relay of the repository (or anything that speaks its contract), paste its wss:// address here, and the next pairing carries it to your phone.
relayConfig.confirmBody: This desktop and your phone will meet at:
relayConfig.confirmCompat: The relay must be compatible with Wolffish — a deployment of the relay in the repository works.
relayConfig.confirmUnpair: Your phone is paired through the current relay and will be unpaired. Pair it again after the change.
relayConfig.invalid: That doesn't look like a relay URL. Use wss://host, or paste your relay's https:// address.

mobile.keyStorage: Pairing keys are stored on this machine using {{backend}}.
mobile.notificationsHint: Lets the agent send a push notification to your paired phone with its notify_phone tool — when a run finishes, fails, or needs you. Nothing is ever sent automatically; the agent has to deliberately call the tool, and Off makes that tool refuse.
mobile.verboseHint: Off keeps the phone's feed clean: replies, delivered files, code edits and shell runs, questions and approvals, reasoning, and errors. On relays every tool call and its result. Connection logging is always on and is not affected by this.
mobile.disconnectHint: Cut the link loose. Your phone reconnects the next time it is opened.
mobile.unpairHint: Forget this phone and drop its keys. Pairing again needs a new QR or code.

web.title: Web UI

disable.title: Turn off the Web UI?
disable.body: This browser is using it. The server stops and this page loses its connection — turn it back on from the desktop app or the wolffish CLI.

web.subtitle: The whole app, served to any browser at this machine's address — a phone on the same network, or a VPS reached by its IP. Same chat, same settings, same agent; protected by one master password.
web.needsPassword: Set a master password below before switching the Web UI on. There is no password-less mode: whoever reaches this address gets the whole agent.
web.httpsHint: Served over HTTPS — notifications and the microphone work in the browser.
web.httpHint: Plain HTTP — HTTPS below for notifications and mic.

password.title: Master password
password.description: What a browser types once to sign in. Wolffish generated a twelve-word passphrase at first launch, so the Web UI could be on from the start; show it, copy it, regenerate it, or replace it with one of your own. Changing it signs every browser out, except the one you change it from.
password.confirmBody: Every other browser that is signed in will be signed out and will need the new password; this one stays signed in.
password.requirements: At least {{min}} characters, rated Good or better: mix letters, numbers and symbols, or use a long passphrase.

hint.length: Make it longer — at least {{min}} characters.
hint.mix: Mix letters, numbers and symbols, or make it a long passphrase.
hint.common: That is a commonly used password — pick something personal.

password.generatedNote: Also shown by wolffish web password.
password.ownNote: Stored hashed, so it cannot be shown here. Regenerate to go back to a passphrase Wolffish can show you.
password.regenerateBody: A new twelve-word passphrase replaces the current one. Every other browser that is signed in will be signed out and will need the new one; this one stays signed in.
password.useOwn: Use a password of my own instead

network.title: Network
network.description: Which port the UI answers on and which addresses it answers at.
network.bindHint: 0.0.0.0 answers on every address this machine has — what a VPS wants. 127.0.0.1 keeps it reachable from this machine only.
network.lowPort: Ports below 1024 need root on Linux (or CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE). Pick a higher port unless Wolffish runs as a service with that right.

https.title: HTTPS
https.description: Browsers only allow notifications, the microphone and installing the app to a home screen on a trusted HTTPS origin. Let's Encrypt can certify a bare public IP address — no domain name needed.

modeHint.off: Plain HTTP. Fine on a trusted local network; notifications and the microphone stay off in the browser.
modeHint.acme: A trusted certificate from Let's Encrypt for this machine's public IP address — or a hostname pointing here — served on port 443, renewed on its own every few days. One button runs the checks, gets the certificate and moves you to https://.
modeHint.selfsigned: A certificate Wolffish mints for itself. Every browser shows a warning once and then proceeds; notifications work on desktop browsers but not on phones, and the app cannot be installed to a home screen.
modeHint.custom: Serve a certificate and key you provide (PEM files on this machine).

https.identifiersHint: The public IP address(es) and/or hostnames browsers will use. Private addresses (192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x) cannot be certified. Comma-separated.
https.detectNone: Could not detect a public address (or it is already listed).
https.httpPortHint: Let's Encrypt connects to port 80 to validate; that listener also redirects browsers to HTTPS. The HTTPS port is 443 unless a pf or iptables forward points elsewhere.
https.acmeIssuing: Asking Let's Encrypt for a certificate…
https.acmeOk: Certificate from Let's Encrypt, valid until {{until}}. Renews itself.
https.ipHint: Detected from the internet. Edit it if this machine is reached at another address. Let's Encrypt must reach ports 80 and 443 at it.
https.domainHint: A hostname that points at this machine gets a normal 90-day certificate instead of the 6-day IP one.
https.staging: Use Let's Encrypt staging (test certificates, no rate limits)
https.fallback: A self-signed certificate is being served until Let's Encrypt issues one; browsers warn until then.

notifications.label: Browser notifications
notifications.description: Lets the agent notify signed-in browsers with its notify_web tool — when a run finishes, fails, or needs you. Delivered as Web Push, so it lands with the tab closed. Off makes the tool refuse.
notifications.testResult: Shown in {{inband}} open browser(s), pushed to {{pushed}}.

verbose.label: Show all tool activity
verbose.description: Same feed preference every channel has. Off shows a clean feed in the browser; On adds every tool call and result.

sessions.title: Signed-in browsers
sessions.description: Every browser that typed the master password. Signing one out ends its session and its notifications.
sessions.none: No browser has signed in yet.

public.title: Public links
public.description: Files, folders and local ports the agent has published at an unguessable URL that needs no sign-in — for people who are not you. Anything else the Web UI serves stays behind the master password.
public.none: Nothing is public. The agent publishes with public_link when a task calls for a link someone else can open.

origin.label: Public address
origin.description: The origin links are handed out at. Leave empty to use this server's own address (the certificate's name under HTTPS, the first reachable address otherwise); set it when a domain or reverse proxy fronts this box.

vps.title: On a server
vps.step1: Install Wolffish on the box and start it as a background service (Settings → Channels → CLI → Start on its own).
vps.step2: The Web UI is already on, behind a master password Wolffish generated — read it with wolffish web password, or Show it here. Wolffish opens its own port in the machine's firewall (ufw, firewalld, Windows Firewall) when it starts; open the port above, and 80 and 443, in your provider's firewall or security group.
vps.step3: On the HTTPS card pick Let's Encrypt, check the detected public IP, press Enable HTTPS and watch the steps — the certificate arrives within a minute, HTTPS answers on 443, and it renews itself.
vps.step4: On your phone, open the address shown above, sign in, allow notifications, and add it to the home screen for a full-screen app.

guide.title: Setting automation times
guide.intro: An automation is a schedule heading plus the prompt underneath it. The heading decides when it runs — use one of these forms:
guide.startup: Runs once every time the app launches.
guide.every: Runs on an interval — minutes (m) or hours (h).
guide.hourly: Runs every hour at that minute.
guide.daily: Runs every day at that time.
guide.dailyTimes: Several times a day: list the times, separated by commas. Every listed time runs.
guide.nightly: Same as Daily — reads better for night times.
guide.weekday: Runs Monday through Friday at that time.
guide.weekly: Runs once a week on that day. Day names are in English.
guide.weeklyDays: Several days a week: list the days, then the time. Add more times after a comma to run each day more than once.
guide.monthly: Runs monthly on that day number. Keep it between 1 and 28 so no month is skipped.
guide.monthlyDays: Several days a month: list the day numbers, then the time. Keep them between 1 and 28.
guide.once: Runs one time at that date, then removes itself.

provider.noProviderDescription: The API provider failed to complete the response — this is not a wolffish issue.
provider.invalidKey: API key invalid or expired — update in settings.
provider.badRequest: The provider rejected the request — try a different model or check your configuration.
provider.modelNotFound: Model not found — may be renamed or retired.
provider.timeout: The provider didn't respond in time — it may be overloaded. Try again or switch providers.
provider.tryAgainMessage: The previous response was cut off by a provider failure ({{reason}}). Pick up where you left off — check what already completed (files written, tool results, plans made) and continue without redoing finished work.
provider.stalled: Five minutes passed with zero response from the API, so the request was aborted. Nothing was lost — Continue picks up from here.
provider.stallContinueMessage: [System: The previous API request was aborted after five minutes with no response from the provider. The conversation continues from here. Everything above — tool results, files written, the plan so far — is still valid; pick up exactly where you left off without redoing finished work, and do not mention this note.]
provider.systemAsideLabel: Continued after the API stopped responding
